patches.from: Grow long-day onions here. They wait for very long summer days (14 to 16 hours) before forming a bulb, which is exactly what this latitude provides. Intermediate-day onions are a reasonable alternative too, especially toward the belt's warmer southern edge. Skip short-day (Southern) onions, which need fall planting and a much milder winter.
patches.value: Grow intermediate-day onions here. They form a bulb at a middle day length, about 12 to 14 hours, which fits this latitude, and they size up best when set out early, so plant from February into late March. Long-day onions also work at the belt's cooler northern edge. Skip short-day (Southern) onions, which are bred for fall planting in much milder winters.

patches.from: This latitude (roughly 37 to 40°N in the Ozark and upland north of the belt) calls for long-day onions, which bulb at 14 to 16 hours of daylight, well matched to the belt's long summer days. Intermediate-day types also perform here and are a reasonable hedge toward the belt's warmer southern edge, where the largest long-day varieties can run short of season. Avoid true short-day (Southern) types, which need a fall planting and a mild winter this belt does not reliably provide.
patches.value: This latitude (roughly 36 to 37°N in the Ozark uplands and the belt's north) is intermediate-day onion country: intermediate types bulb at 12 to 14 hours of daylight, the belt's early-summer day length, and they build the most size when set out early, so aim for February into late March rather than April. Long-day types remain a reasonable choice at the belt's cooler northern edge in southern Missouri. Avoid true short-day (Southern) types, which are bred for a fall planting and a mild winter this belt does not reliably provide. University of Arkansas guidance lists intermediate-day onions as suited to the northern half of the state, and Tennessee and Oklahoma Extension both recommend intermediate-day for dry bulbs.

patches.value: This belt (roughly 34 to 35°N in the Delta lowlands) sits in intermediate-day onion country, below the 36°N line where growers switch off long-day types. patches.from: Onion in the Mid-South is a single spring-planted crop with no fall crop. Set sets or seedlings out as soon as the soil is workable, well ahead of the last frost since onion is cold-hardy, roughly mid February into mid April in zone 8 and about a week and a half later in the cooler zone 7 uplands. This belt spans long-day onion territory: the cooler Ozark uplands sit squarely in long-day country, while the lowland South sits at the warm edge of it, where intermediate-day types are an equally strong choice and the largest long-day varieties can run short of season. Avoid true short-day (Southern) types, which need fall planting and a milder winter than this belt reliably offers. Bulbing is triggered by day length rather than by planting date, so bulbs mature on roughly the same midsummer calendar regardless of exactly when they went in; lift and cure two to four weeks before storage.
patches.value: Onion in the Mid-South is a single spring-planted crop with no fall crop. Set sets or seedlings out as soon as the soil is workable, roughly mid February into late March in zone 8 and about a week and a half later in the cooler zone 7 uplands; intermediate-day onions size up best when set early, so the window closes by the end of March rather than running into April. Onion is cold-hardy and goes in well before the last frost. Bulbing is triggered by day length rather than by planting date, so bulbs mature on roughly the same midsummer calendar regardless of exactly when they went in; lift and cure two to four weeks before storage. University of Arkansas, Oklahoma State, and University of Tennessee Extension all steer this belt to short-day or intermediate-day onions.
